subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: A Tour Around My Village — Students observe the picture of Chandan's village and describe what they see (p. 4)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the opening story of Chandan's village, then asks children to look carefully at the village scene in Textbook p. 4 — who they spot, where each person or place is, what seems to be happening.

Children write their observations in their notebooks in response to the prompt on Textbook p. 4: 'What do you see in the picture? Describe below.' Teacher circulates, nudging children to notice specific details — the well, the post office, the banyan tree, the health centre.

Pairs share their descriptions briefly. Teacher invites two or three children to read aloud what they wrote, then draws attention to how different people and places they noticed depend on each other — the shopkeeper needs the road, the school needs the health centre nearby.

Children add one sentence to their notebooks naming one connection they had not noticed before. Teacher asks: 'What would happen to Chandan's village if the well disappeared?' — leaving the question open as a prompt for the next encounter with this idea.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a community scene and describe how places and people are connected to each other.
periods.section_context: Chandan's village scene illustration; playground, post office, well, banyan tree, health centre, school, shopkeeper, road, police
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Who uses the banyan tree? Who uses the well? Do the same people use both?' to draw out that shared spaces serve the whole community, not just one group. Where children name a traditional water source or gathering place from their own locality, welcome it naturally into the discussion.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Tour Around My Village — Students explore their own locality and record how people and places are connected in a table (p. 4)

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the village scene children observed earlier (the well, shopkeeper, school, health centre) and asks: 'Does your own locality have places like these? Which ones?' Children call out answers briefly to warm up.

Children draw a simple two-column table in their notebooks (Place or Person | How they are connected to others) following the prompt in Textbook p. 4. They fill in at least four rows using people and places from their own neighbourhood — home, school, market, temple or mosque, health centre, etc.

Small groups of three share their tables and look for entries that appear in more than one child's notebook — these are the places the whole community depends on. A spokesperson from each group shares one shared-dependence finding with the class.

Teacher closes by asking: 'Which one place in your locality, if it closed, would affect the most people?' Children write their one-sentence answer. Teacher affirms that communities are built on these shared, mutually dependent spaces.

periods.implied_lo: Students can collect and organise observations about their immediate environment in a structured table and identify patterns of interdependence.
periods.section_context: Students' own locality; local places and people mapped into a connections table
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If children struggle to see connections, ask 'Who built the road? Who uses it? Who repairs it?' as a worked example before they write. Accept any locally relevant place names — panchayat office, masjid, gurudwara, hand-pump — as fully valid entries.

periods.activity_title: Van Mahotsav Poster — Why Shared Places Matter
periods.section_ref: Van Mahotsav: A Festival for Planting Trees
periods.textbook_anchor: Van Mahotsav: A Festival for Planting Trees — Students create a colourful poster to invite the neighbourhood to participate in Van Mahotsav (p. 6)
materials: A4 or half-chart paper (one per pair)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Van Mahotsav passage aloud and opens the discussion questions from Textbook p. 5 orally: Why are parks, schools, hospitals, and bus stops important? What would change if one disappeared? What can we do to keep them clean? Children respond in pairs, then share one idea each.

Children work in pairs to create a colourful Van Mahotsav invitation poster as described in Textbook p. 6 — inviting neighbours to plant trees and care for shared spaces. Each poster must include the name of the festival, a reason to come, and a picture of something they want to protect (a tree, a park, a well).

Pairs hold up their posters. Teacher invites three pairs to explain: 'What did you choose to draw, and why is that place or thing worth protecting?' The class listens and any pair may add a quick verbal agreement or a different reason.

Teacher closes by asking: 'Van Mahotsav happens every year in July — why do you think a whole week is set aside just for planting trees?' Children respond briefly. Teacher affirms that returning to care for nature every year is itself a community tradition.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express understanding of why shared public spaces matter by creating a persuasive visual communication piece.
periods.section_context: Van Mahotsav (1–7 July); parks, schools, hospitals, bus stops as shared public spaces; invitation poster for tree-planting festival
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Before poster-making, ask 'Has your family ever gone to a park or planted a tree together — what was it like?' to ground the activity in real experience. If a child mentions a local tree-planting tradition or seasonal planting practice, invite them to include that on their poster.

periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Hands in the Community — Students list the work, materials, tools, and skills needed to develop and maintain a park, using a mason as the given example (p. 8)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 7–8 illustration of community members under the banyan tree

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the village scene from Textbook p. 7: parents and community members gathering under the banyan tree to plan the Van Mahotsav — the carpenter, electrician, and Noor the nursery owner each bringing a different skill. Children name any similar people they have seen working in their own area.

Children open Textbook p. 8 and copy the table structure into their notebooks: Work | Materials | Tools | Skills. They complete at least four rows for different workers who might help develop or maintain a park (carpenter, electrician, plumber, gardener, sweeper, painter). The mason row from the textbook is the worked example.

Children compare their tables with a neighbour and add any worker the neighbour included that they did not. Teacher asks: 'Did anyone list a worker who uses no tools at all? Is there any work that needs no skill?' — opening up discussion of invisible skills like cooking, managing, or storytelling.

Teacher closes with: 'If one of these workers was absent, what would not get done?' Children name one worker and the gap their absence would leave. Teacher affirms that every skill is part of a chain — the community depends on all of them together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify different kinds of community work by the materials, tools, and skills each requires.
periods.section_context: Carpenter, electrician, plant nursery owner (Noor), mason; park development and maintenance; tools, materials, and skills table
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Does your family member use a tool for their work? What is it?' before children fill in the table, so they can draw on familiar examples. If children name traditional craft workers — potters, weavers, bangle makers — affirm these as equally valid examples of skilled community helpers.

periods.activity_title: Work Interview — Asking the Right Questions
periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Hands in the Community — Students find out from family members or neighbours about their work using guiding questions (p. 8)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the three guiding interview questions from Textbook p. 8 aloud: What do you like most about your work? What tools or things do you use? What challenges do you face? Children discuss in pairs: 'Have you ever asked a family member these questions? What do you think they would say?'

Each child picks one person they know — a parent, neighbour, relative, or school staff member — and writes that person's name and occupation in their notebook. They then write their own answer to each of the three questions, imagining or recalling what that person might say, based on what they know of the work.

Groups of four share their chosen workers. One child in each group acts as the 'worker' and the others ask the three questions as an in-class role-play. The 'worker' answers in character. Teacher circulates, asking groups: 'What surprised you about that job? Is it harder or easier than it looks?'

Whole-class close: teacher invites two children to share one thing they learned about a worker's challenges. Teacher asks: 'Do we always notice how much work goes into keeping a community running?' Children write one sentence of appreciation in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can formulate and use inquiry questions to find out about the work and challenges of people in their community.
periods.section_context: Interview inquiry about community workers; questions about tools, skills, and challenges; family members and neighbours as informants
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'What is one job in your locality that you think is overlooked — that people do not say thank you for?' to surface the idea that all work has dignity regardless of status. Encourage children who mention traditional or artisan occupations to describe what makes that work special in their community.

periods.activity_title: Community Solidarity — The Chinar Bridge Story
periods.textbook_anchor: Celebrating Van Mahotsav — Students discuss whether communities coming together in times of need is important, and recall one such occasion from their locality (p. 10)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 9–10 illustration of Van Mahotsav celebration and Kanker bridge building

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Kanker, Chhattisgarh story from Textbook p. 9–10 aloud: the whole community building a bamboo-and-stone bridge over the flooded Chinar river in two days so students and villagers could cross safely. Children listen, then name one thing about the story that surprised or moved them.

Teacher poses the discussion question from Textbook p. 10: 'It is important for communities to come together in times of need — what do you think about this statement?' Children discuss in groups of three, with one child noting their group's key reason on a scrap of paper.

Groups share their key reason. Teacher collects the reasons on the board, grouping them roughly (safety / efficiency / emotional support / belonging). Teacher then poses the second question from Textbook p. 10: 'Do people in your locality come together and support each other? Can you remember one occasion?' Children share briefly.

Each child writes two to three sentences in their notebook: the occasion they recalled and what made it possible — what did people bring (time, skill, materials, food) that they could not have provided alone? Teacher closes: 'What is the difference between a community and a crowd?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain, with a real or recalled example, why collective action makes a community stronger than individual effort alone.
periods.section_context: Van Mahotsav celebration with cleaning, planting, watering, cooking groups; Kanker Chhattisgarh bamboo-and-stone bridge over Chinar river (2024); community solidarity in times of need
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a child recalls a local flood, harvest, or festival where the community pulled together, draw that story out — it makes the Kanker bridge example concrete and local. Ask: 'Who led the bridge-building? Did they need one leader or many?' to open up discussion of distributed leadership in community work.

periods.activity_title: Shared Feast — Nature, Food, and Festival Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Sharing a Meal — Students write about how their family or community works together while preparing for a festival or occasion (p. 11)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 11 illustration of communal feast on banana leaves

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the post-plantation feast from Textbook p. 11 — vegetables and cereals contributed by all, served on banana leaves, and the leaves afterwards composted in a pit to enrich the soil. Teacher asks: 'Why do you think they used banana leaves instead of plates? What happens to the leaves after?' Children discuss briefly.

Teacher introduces the Uruka celebration from Textbook p. 11 — the first day of Magh Bihu in Assam on 14 January, where communities build a bamboo-and-hay hut called Bhela Ghar and share a communal feast. Teacher asks: 'Has anyone heard of Magh Bihu or a similar harvest festival? What do people eat or do together at such times in your family?' Children share in pairs.

Children write in their notebooks in response to the prompt from Textbook p. 11: 'How do you work together as a family or community while preparing for a festival or occasion?' They describe who does what — who cooks, who cleans, who decorates, who brings things, who invites guests — and note if any special food or material (like a leaf, a grain, a flower) is used.

Three or four children share their written responses. Teacher draws out the connection: 'In the village feast, the banana leaf feeds people and then feeds the soil. Is there anything in your festival preparation that goes back to nature?' Children note one idea. Teacher affirms that traditional practices often carry this kind of circular care for nature.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how cultural practices and food traditions connect community life to the natural environment.
periods.section_context: Post-plantation communal feast on banana leaves; banana-leaf composting for manure; Uruka (Magh Bihu, 14 January, Assam); Bhela Ghar (bamboo-and-hay hut); festival food and cooperative preparation
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Does your family use any plant — a leaf, a flower, a grain — in a special way during festivals?' to draw out local food and nature traditions naturally. If children mention Pongal, Onam, Lohri, Bihu, or any regional harvest practice, affirm all as examples of the same pattern: communities celebrating nature's gifts together.

periods.activity_title: Our School, Our Team — Roles, Riddles, and a Community Action
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students write the different roles people play in their school community (p. 13)
materials: natural materials for artefact option — leaves, twigs, seeds (only if option c is chosen)
small broom or dustpan (only if option b is chosen)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 13–16 reflection pages including school roles diagram and riddle pictures

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 13 and write the roles of different people in their school — teachers, students, caretakers, bus drivers, administrative staff — noting what each person does and why the school would not function without them. Teacher connects this to the Khetala practice from Sikkim, mentioned in the section: agricultural specialists who come together at harvest to help each other, showing that cooperative role-sharing is an old and widespread tradition.

Groups of four or five choose one activity from Textbook p. 14: (a) a brief symbolic tree plantation using a seed or seedling if available, or drawing and labelling a tree they would like to plant; (b) a quick classroom cleanliness drive; or (c) making a simple artefact from natural materials (a leaf arrangement or a twig-and-seed decoration). Each group names their activity and does it together.

Children open Textbook p. 15 and solve the community-place riddles, matching each clue to the picture. Then each child writes one new riddle about a public place of their own choice on Textbook p. 16, following the same format. Two or three children read their riddles aloud for the class to guess.

Teacher asks the two closing discussion questions from Textbook p. 13: 'What are ways we can take care of nature and our neighbourhood?' and 'How does helping others and working together make our community better?' Children share one answer each briefly. Teacher closes: 'Every person in a community — whether they plant a tree, sweep a path, or carry a message — is part of the same team.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and articulate the roles of different community members and practise a shared act of care for their immediate environment.
periods.section_context: School community roles (teachers, students, caretakers, bus drivers); Khetala harvest cooperation (Sikkim); group activity choices (tree plantation, cleanliness drive, nature artefact); community-place riddles; public place riddle writing
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'What skill or craft is your family known for? Has anyone learned it from an elder?' to connect the T-20 craft inquiry naturally — children who mention basket-making, pottery, wall painting, or weaving are sharing exactly what the section calls for. If a child's riddle names a local place others do not know, invite them to describe it briefly so the class learns something new about their own community.

assessment_items.question_text: In Chandan's village, the banyan tree is a place where elders gather. Which of the following best describes why a space like this is important for a community?

options.label: A
options.text: It gives shade so that people do not feel hot.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a shared space where people meet, talk, and make decisions together.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the oldest tree in the village and people respect old things.

options.label: D
options.text: It marks the boundary between one part of the village and another.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item assesses whether students understood the observation activity — that shared spaces serve the whole community's social and civic life, not merely a physical purpose.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a community scene and describe how places and people are connected to each other.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student reduced the banyan tree's role to a physical comfort function, missing the social and civic significance of shared community spaces discussed in the observation activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student focused on age or heritage as the reason for respect — a plausible but incomplete reading that does not capture the idea of shared use and mutual dependence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused a shared gathering space with a boundary marker, suggesting they did not distinguish between places that divide and places that unite community members.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya explored her locality and noticed a hand-pump, a primary school, a small market, and a health centre. She wants to record how these places are connected to each other. Choose any two of these places and explain how each one is connected to the people or to the other places in the locality.
expected_elements: Names two places from the given list (hand-pump, primary school, small market, health centre).
For each place, states at least one connection — who uses it, who maintains it, or how it depends on or supports another place or person.
Shows that both places serve more than one person or group (i.e., they are shared resources), not just a single individual.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two places. Connections may be simple and concrete — 'the hand-pump gives water to everyone who comes to the market too' is fully valid. Award credit for any reasonable, logical connection grounded in how the community uses these spaces. Regionally varied place names (well, tubewell, anganwadi, masjid) are equally acceptable — the named list is illustrative, not exhaustive.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can collect and organise observations about their immediate environment in a structured table and identify patterns of interdependence.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

expected_elements: Names two places from the given list (hand-pump, primary school, small market, health centre).
For each place, states at least one connection — who uses it, who maintains it, or how it depends on or supports another place or person.
Shows that both places serve more than one person or group (i.e., they are shared resources), not just a single individual.

assessment_items.task: Think about a park, a school, or a community well in your area that you feel is important. Make a small poster (drawing plus words) that invites people in your neighbourhood to help take care of it. Your poster should show: (a) the name or picture of the place, (b) one reason why this place matters for everyone, and (c) one thing people can do to keep it clean or safe.
assessment_items.scaffold: Start by drawing the place in the centre of your paper. Around it, write the name of the place and one reason it is important. At the bottom, write or draw one action people can take — planting a tree, not littering, watering plants, etc.
format_of_output: A drawing of the chosen community space
One written or dictated reason the place matters
One written or drawn action people can take to protect it
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any locally meaningful community space — a hand-pump, a masjid courtyard, a chaupal, a neighbourhood park. The poster need not be elaborate; a simple drawing with legible words or a dictated sentence is sufficient. Regional variation in place names and actions is expected and fully valid.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Van Mahotsav: A Festival for Planting Trees
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express understanding of why shared public spaces matter by creating a persuasive visual communication piece.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can identify a shared natural or community resource, articulate why it matters to more than one person, and propose a concrete conservation or care action — combining the persuasive and the civic.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides children to put the place at the centre, reason around it, and close with an action — mirroring the Van Mahotsav poster structure from the activity. A child who follows this flow has met the implied_lo even if their writing is minimal.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: poster clearly names the place, gives a community-level reason (not just personal preference), and proposes a specific, doable action. Weak: drawing only with no reason or action; reason is purely personal ('I like it there') with no community dimension; action is vague ('be good').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who cannot write independently may dictate their reason and action to the teacher or a peer. Children who draw fluently but struggle with words may use speech bubbles or single-word labels. All formats are valid as long as the three components are present in some form.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The poster format directly mirrors the Van Mahotsav invitation activity and allows children who express themselves visually to demonstrate the same competency as those who write well.

assessment_items.question_text:
A community wants to build a new park. Look at the list of workers below and answer the questions.

Workers: Mason, Carpenter, Electrician, Gardener

(a) Name ONE material and ONE tool that the carpenter would use.
(b) Name ONE skill the electrician must have to do their job safely.
expected_elements: For the carpenter: names at least one material (wood, timber, planks, nails) and at least one tool (hammer, saw, chisel, screwdriver).
For the electrician: names a skill directly related to safe electrical work (knowledge of wiring, ability to test circuits, understanding of safety precautions, ability to identify faults).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any correct material-tool pair for the carpenter; regional names for tools are valid (e.g., 'randa' for a hand plane). For the electrician skill, accept any response that shows awareness of technical or safety knowledge — 'knowing how wires work' or 'being careful with live wires' are both creditable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify different kinds of community work by the materials, tools, and skills each requires.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

For the electrician: names a skill directly related to safe electrical work (knowledge of wiring, ability to test circuits, understanding of safety precautions, ability to identify faults).

assessment_items.question_text: Priya wants to find out about the work of the vegetable seller in her market. She decides to ask three questions. Write the three questions Priya should ask, and then explain what she hopes to learn from the answers that she could not learn just by watching the seller work.
look_for: Three distinct, open-ended questions — not yes/no — that probe different aspects of the work (tools or materials used, challenges faced, what the person enjoys, how they learned the skill, etc.).
At least one question that goes beyond visible action to ask about experience, challenge, or knowledge (e.g., 'What is the hardest part of your work?').

An explanation that names at least one kind of knowledge that observation alone cannot reveal — for example, the seller's daily challenges, how they learned pricing, where they get their vegetables from, or what they enjoy about their work.
The response shows an understanding that inquiry through questions gives different information than silent observation.
assessment_items.annotation: Do not penalise children who write simple but genuine questions. The key quality marker is whether the third bullet is addressed — does the child name something that watching cannot reveal? Accept regionally varied examples of market workers (fish seller, grain seller, flower seller).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can formulate and use inquiry questions to find out about the work and challenges of people in their community.

assessment_items.question_text: In Kanker, Chhattisgarh, the whole community built a bamboo-and-stone bridge over the flooded Chinar river in just two days. Which of the following best explains why the community was able to finish the bridge so quickly?

options.label: A
options.text: One very skilled engineer planned and built the whole bridge by himself.

options.label: B
options.text: The government sent machines and workers to build the bridge for the village.

options.label: C
options.text: Many people worked together, each contributing their skill, time, or materials.

options.label: D
options.text: Bamboo and stone are very easy materials to work with, so any one person could build it fast.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. This item checks whether students grasped the core argument of the Celebrating Van Mahotsav section — that collective effort, not individual heroism or external help, is what makes community action effective.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain, with a real or recalled example, why collective action makes a community stronger than individual effort alone.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student attributed the success to individual expertise rather than collective effort, missing the chapter's central theme of community solidarity and distributed contribution.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student assumed external governmental intervention was the cause, failing to recognise that the chapter explicitly presents community self-organisation as the reason the bridge was built.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student focused on the material properties rather than the human factor, suggesting they noticed the building materials mentioned in the story but did not engage with the social argument about collective action.

assessment_items.question_text:
The community in Chandan's village served their post-plantation meal on banana leaves and then composted those leaves in a pit. In Assam, during Magh Bihu (Uruka), communities build a Bhela Ghar from bamboo and hay and share a feast together.

(a) What does the banana-leaf composting practice show about how the community cares for the land?
(b) What is one way in which the Uruka celebration and the Van Mahotsav feast are similar?
expected_elements: For (a): states that composting the banana leaves returns nutrients to the soil or improves soil quality — showing that a natural material is used and then given back to nature, rather than wasted.

For (b): identifies a genuine similarity — both involve a communal feast shared by many people, both use natural materials (banana leaf / bamboo and hay), both happen after a collective act of work or seasonal change, or both connect food and community celebration to the natural environment.
assessment_items.annotation: For (a), accept any response that conveys the circular, waste-reducing logic of composting — 'the leaves go back to the earth' is sufficient. For (b), accept any valid similarity; there is more than one correct answer. A student who names a local harvest festival they know personally and draws a parallel to Uruka should receive full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how cultural practices and food traditions connect community life to the natural environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

assessment_items.task: Think about your school. Different people make the school work every day — teachers, students, caretakers, cooks, bus drivers, office staff. Choose one person whose work is often not noticed, and write a short appreciation note (4–6 sentences) to them. In your note, (a) name their role, (b) describe what they do that keeps the school running, and (c) explain why the school would be different without their work.
assessment_items.scaffold: Start with: 'Dear [name of role], I want to thank you for...' Then describe one or two specific things they do. End with: 'Without your work, our school would...'
format_of_output: A short written appreciation note of 4–6 sentences
Addressed to a named school role
Includes a description of the person's work
Includes a statement about why the school needs their contribution
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any school role the child chooses, including roles not listed in the prompt (gardener, security guard, librarian, mid-day meal cook). The note need not be formally structured — credit the content. A child who can articulate why the role matters to the whole community has met the implied_lo.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and articulate the roles of different community members and practise a shared act of care for their immediate environment.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can recognise that a school functions because of many interdependent roles, name the specific contribution of an often-overlooked member, and articulate why that contribution matters for the whole community — demonstrating the civic disposition the section builds toward.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The 'Dear... / without your work...' frame gives children a manageable entry point. A child who fills all three scaffold parts (role, what they do, why the school needs them) has addressed all three elements of the implied_lo. Read for substance, not for sentence count.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific, often-overlooked role; describes concrete daily actions (sweeping classrooms, cooking mid-day meals, driving children safely); clearly articulates a community-level impact (other students can learn, children are fed, the campus is clean). Weak: chooses a prominent role like the principal with only generic praise; describes only one action with no community-level reasoning; note is purely emotional ('you are nice') without any description of the work.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who struggle to write may dictate their note to the teacher. Children who prefer to draw may submit an annotated drawing (with the three elements labelled) instead of prose. The intended recipient of the note may be any person in the school community — rigid adherence to the listed roles is not required.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Short appreciation note (written prose or annotated drawing)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The appreciation-note format requires children to address a real person in their immediate community, making the reflection concrete and personal rather than abstract — directly serving the R&A dominant mode of the period.
